judgments.why: Y is a long, digressive, slightly awkward machine-translated letter with details the card lacks (the iron obelisk, Wolff's joke, chicory coffee, Schulze), while X is a short, tidy 'My dearest Marie' pastiche that just restates the card and adds a sneer.

X has Hegel's dry joke about 'the interests of Mrs. Hegel' and the rough syntax of a machine translation; Y adds invented colour (frying onions, Burgundy, a room by the Seine) in the stock LLM letter frame.

X is long and full of particulars the card does not give (a 25-franc fare to Paris, the three-master pictured as a Sultan, Potter and Berghem, Mrs. Voss, his neckerchief); Y is a generic, sour pastiche with an invented price.

Y has telling particulars (Besseling is a stricter Catholic than van Ghert, so fish both times, and the town hall as the ideal of a free burgher city), while X invents a price, warm wine and a trip to Utrecht.
X is a brief, wry real aside ('I myself have only known it for half an hour'), whereas Y invents an innkeeper named Kral, mutton, a price and moralising about the sons.

Y has the machine-translation slip 'my cousin' for Cousin and Hegel's own comparison of the Champs Élysées to the Berlin Tents and its crowds of philistines, while X is formulaic and invents soup and a sneer at Cousin.
Y is a hurried, emotional real fragment (relief at the letters, apprehension about Monday), while X adds invented colour (beer tasting of tar, three thalers, 'your snuff and your sharp tongue').
X is a terse note-like fragment with a real comparison to the Peacock Island and its georginas and altheas, whereas Y invents a price, a cake and a quarrel with a Prague professor about Fries.

X has rich, idiosyncratic detail (four woollen layers against the cold, the Goethe package, reluctance about the journey, the Peter joke, a comparison with the Nuremberg churches); Y compresses the card and adds an invented meal and price.
Y has an authentic, tender fatherly passage on being 'an old father' and on Immanuel's birthday, while X invents a Café de Paris dinner, prices and a snuff box.
Y has a garbled playbill quote ('/67 o'clock') and Hegel's real enthusiasm for the singers' antique heads; X invents a price and a meal and calls Lablache a bore.
X is a brief, reflective real fragment on the small French theatres being 'jokes one quickly gets over'; Y uses the LLM frame and invents a two-franc seat, damp wool and advice to the boys.
Y is a short real sentence with the 'my dear' turn and joy at her letter; X invents a three-kreuzer bottle of water, students playing whist and worn shoes.
Y has a real, warm wish that the children and his wife could see the Magic Pear again; X invents chestnuts, Zweigelt wine, a meeting with Schuster and a new coat.
Y has particulars (getting up at 3, hilly road, finding acquaintances everywhere, the Moselle vineyards), while X garbles the timeline and adds a generic meal and musings.
Y is a long, detailed real narrative (Elberfeld, Egmont at Kassel, the deaf Grand Duke, the Griesheims, the Schwendlers), whereas X condenses the card and invents a six-thaler lunch.
Y is a short real closing written at the table ('we are sitting at the table'), while X uses the LLM frame and adds roast beef, a 'modest sum' and reflections on the state.
Y has idiosyncratic real detail (wood-carved confessionals, the English greeting in Nuremberg, a joke about sweating at Waterloo), while X is a generic summary with the stock closing.

X has Hegel's apology to the Prussian postal service after his earlier complaint and the route details, whereas Y invents a missing coachman, a two-thaler lunch and calls the painting merely competent.
Y is a brief, faithful real note (again 'friend and cousin' for Cousin), while X contradicts the card with a dinner and an afternoon meeting and invents prices and a cravat.
Y is a dated real postscript with an affectionate 'so near am I to you, my dearest', while X pads the card with commentary on Romantics, room prices and the boys.

X is a fragmentary real text that begins mid-sentence and has specifics (the Battle of Culm, the eye-water that did him good, plans for the castle hill), while Y invents a duck, a price and 'iron and regret'.

Y has real playful family asides (a pun on Marienschein meaning her, the boys told to check the Seven Years' War map, the 'Zierlisel') and starts mid-text, while X invents a duck, a price and 'your snuff'.

X is a long, vivid real account (the clipped Augarten trees, the Leopoldsberg view, Rembold as a fellow Swabian, walking home by moonlight), while Y is a dismissive pastiche with invented prices and fish.
